title: Release the R3F WebGL renderer at real page teardown boundaries

scope.subject: Prevent SwiftShader GPU/context accumulation between hosted Playwright BrowserContexts by releasing the existing R3F-owned WebGL renderer when a document is actually discarded

research_summary: Hosted evidence now shows browser.newContext timeouts and Chromium SharedImageManager mailbox errors after only a few otherwise ordinary WebGL cases, even after the live Surface visual was isolated. React Three Fiber already owns the single Three.js WebGLRenderer and disposes it on normal React unmount; the gap is abrupt document teardown, where React cleanup is not a reliable release boundary. Reuse the existing R3F renderer through useThree, listen only for non-persisted pagehide, and invoke Three.js forceContextLoss plus dispose at that terminal page boundary. WEBGL_lose_context is specifically documented to destroy the underlying graphics context and graphics resources. Do not add a second renderer, GPU manager, custom animation loop, unload handler, or browser runner. For hosted validation, wrap Playwright's existing page fixture so each test signals that same terminal release contract before the framework closes its BrowserContext; this keeps Playwright as the browser/test lifecycle owner while making GPU release deterministic.

sources.finding: R3F Canvas owns the WebGLRenderer it creates and automatically disposes it on normal unmount; use the existing Canvas renderer instead of creating a second lifecycle owner.
Three.js WebGLRenderer exposes dispose() to free renderer GPU resources and forceContextLoss() to deliberately lose the underlying WebGL context.
WEBGL_lose_context.loseContext() destroys the underlying graphics context and all graphics resources and is the recommended mechanism for programmatically halting WebGL use.
pagehide is the browser lifecycle event intended for navigation-away handling and PageTransitionEvent.persisted distinguishes bfcache retention from an actually discarded document.
Three.js GPU allocations are not automatically released for library objects; geometry, material, render-target and pass disposal remains required throughout the normal component lifecycle.
Playwright fixtures can wrap built-in fixtures and execute deterministic teardown after the test body while leaving browser and BrowserContext ownership with Playwright.

search_ladder.conclusion: The product already has a single R3F Canvas and renderer; this unit is a terminal lifecycle correction, not a renderer or application replacement.

Keep R3F as renderer owner and Playwright as browser owner: useThree supplies the existing renderer, while a wrapped page fixture invokes the product terminal-release contract before BrowserContext teardown.
Three.js already exposes the resource disposal primitives, so a separate GPU-resource registry or renderer lifecycle subsystem would duplicate framework ownership.
Use the standard context-loss extension through Three.js forceContextLoss at non-persisted pagehide, while preserving bfcache pages.

candidates.name: Existing R3F-owned WebGLRenderer plus a terminal pagehide lifecycle hook
candidates.source: Current single Canvas renderer exposed by useThree, with Three.js renderer disposal primitives
candidates.reason: R3F already owns normal unmount disposal; adding one bounded non-persisted pagehide hook closes the abrupt-document teardown gap without creating another renderer or resource manager.

candidates.name: Standard WEBGL_lose_context terminal release
candidates.reason: It destroys the underlying graphics context and graphics resources at the exact terminal boundary that hosted SwiftShader evidence shows is leaking across BrowserContexts.

candidates.name: Playwright wrapped page fixture for deterministic pre-context GPU release
candidates.reason: It runs teardown before Playwright closes the BrowserContext, giving the application a deterministic terminal lifecycle signal without manually launching Chromium or replacing native context isolation.

candidates.name: Project-owned GPU resource registry and browser teardown manager
candidates.reason: It would duplicate R3F and Three.js ownership, require every renderer asset to register twice, and still rely on the same browser WebGL context at teardown.

decision.rationale: Keep the current single R3F Canvas and all existing per-object disposal. Add one shared terminal-release contract: non-persisted pagehide invokes it in the product, and a wrapped Playwright page fixture invokes the same contract immediately before BrowserContext teardown. The contract force-loses and disposes the existing renderer so SwiftShader resources are destroyed before Chromium reuses the browser process, while persisted bfcache pages and the real-GPU rendering path remain unchanged.
decision.fallback: If Chromium still accumulates SwiftShader resources after explicit page-terminal release, recycle Playwright worker/browser processes at measured boundaries using native projects rather than serializing the whole suite or adding global timeout.
